title: Towards High-Fidelity CAD Generation via LLM-Driven Program Generation and Text-Based B-Rep Primitive Grounding
one_liner: Generate a CAD program and then ground its shape references to the right faces, edges, and solids so that advanced operations run on the intended parts.
lead: Modern CAD work mixes two things that must agree: a step-by-step construction program and the concrete shape pieces that each step touches. Many systems handle those parts separately, which breaks down on industrial designs because later operations such as fillets and chamfers only work when the program points at the right geometric pieces. FutureCAD joins program writing with geometric grounding, because the generated script is only useful if each operation acts on the intended faces, edges, and bodies.

problem.h2: Why text-to-CAD breaks on real feature-based design
paras: A realistic CAD object is not only a final shape. It is also a sequence of operations such as sketching, extruding, cutting, rounding, and beveling. Those operations depend on exact geometric selections, so a later step can fail even when the earlier text description was mostly understood.

Many earlier systems choose between two incomplete views. One view writes a construction program but struggles to point at the right geometric pieces. The other view tries to produce the final boundary shape directly but loses the editable feature sequence. Industrial design needs both, because engineers want a script that runs and a model that stays editable.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Write an executable CadQuery script and let a separate grounding module map text references such as rounded top edge or inner side face to the actual geometric pieces that the script should use.

paras: The paper changes the interface between program writing and shape editing. Instead of forcing the writer to produce fragile low-level selections directly, it lets the writer name geometric targets in text and hands those names to a grounding module.
object.object: the link between a generated CAD program and the exact shape pieces that each later step should modify

hidden.name: which exact geometric primitive each high-level edit is supposed to touch
paras: The hardest missing fact is not the broad object category. It is the exact local target of each edit. When a user asks for a rounded outer corner or a beveled inner rim, the system must decide which edge or face that phrase refers to inside the current partially built shape.

FutureCAD makes that hidden choice explicit. The writer states the intended target in words, and the grounding module resolves that description against the current shape state. This helps because many later CAD operations fail only when the local target is wrong, even if the rest of the script is reasonable.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the local geometric choices that matter most for advanced operations.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the exact face, edge, or body that each edit step is supposed to use.
The method closes the gap between feature programs and boundary shape detail by grounding text descriptions of primitives to the current model state.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: separate writing the plan from choosing the exact shape target
paras: Program writing and geometric grounding are related but not identical jobs. A single writer can describe the intended construction sequence, yet still struggle to point at the exact local shape piece after several earlier edits have changed the shape. The two-part design helps because the writer handles the high-level sequence while the grounding module resolves local references against the current shape.

The new dataset and reward-based training matter as well. Real industrial models contain the complicated feature interactions that toy shape collections miss, so training on those cases teaches the system where local geometric references become difficult. The reward phase then favors scripts that actually execute and match the target object, because a good script must stay valid all the way through the final edit.

An executable script that edits the intended shape pieces because both parts now agree

math.h2: Reward scripts that both run and pick the right shape pieces
math.words: A compact summary is to score a generated CAD script by asking whether it executes successfully, whether its grounded selections are correct, and whether the final shape matches the target design.
math.equation: cad_score(script) = execute_ok(script) + alpha * grounding_match(script) + beta * shape_match(script)
symbols: overall value of one generated CAD program
whether the script runs without failure
how often the text-based selections land on the intended faces, edges, or bodies
how closely the final constructed object matches the target design
weights on selection quality and final shape quality

lines: Script A runs, but it rounds the wrong outer edge.

math.note: The paper uses a fuller training setup, but this summary captures the main idea that executable code alone is not enough when local shape references are wrong.

charts.title: Separated program-or-shape baselines
charts.note: Baselines lose accuracy on real designs because they either miss the editable feature sequence or miss the exact geometric targets.

charts.title: FutureCAD
charts.note: The paper reports stronger results because the writer and the grounding module solve different parts of the problem and reinforce each other.

items.b: Text descriptions can still be ambiguous.
items.html: If several edges fit the same phrase, grounding may choose the wrong one because the request did not include enough local detail.

items.b: Early script mistakes can corrupt later grounding.
items.html: A wrong extrude or cut changes the partial shape, so later face and edge references may stop matching the intended object.

items.b: Real CAD systems contain tool-specific quirks.
items.html: A script that works in one construction library may still need adaptation elsewhere because operation semantics can differ across tools.
The framework matters because it turns geometric selection into an explicit learned step instead of hoping the writer gets every local reference correct by chance.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a text-to-CAD demo with tasks that require local feature edits such as fillets, chamfers, holes, and cutouts. Compare a plain script writer against a FutureCAD-style system that writes the script and then grounds text descriptions of geometric targets before execution.

The demo should log three things: whether the script runs, whether each local selection hits the intended primitive, and how close the final object is to the target model. The grounded system should win because correct local references prevent later edit steps from drifting onto the wrong shape piece.
demo.metric_eq: grounding_gain = primitive_match_futurecad - primitive_match_baseline ; fidelity_gain = shape_match_futurecad - shape_match_baseline
demo.closing: The point of the demo is to show that editable CAD generation depends on both a correct program and correct geometric grounding.
